extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates learning algebraic geometry (schemes and morphisms)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, properties, examples, and exercises about morphisms of schemes (quasicompact, quasiseparated, affine, finite, integral, finite type/presentation, quasiﬁnite), plus key theorems (Qcqs Lemma, Generic Freeness, Chevalley) and elimination theory. Intended as a textbook section to teach and test understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicompact morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y of schemes is quasicompact if for every open affine subset U of Y, π^{-1}(U) is quasicompact. (Equivalently, the preimage of any quasi-compact open subset is quasicompact.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation: finiteness conveniences (finite sets have maxima, inductive proofs). Use in practice: many reasonable schemes are quasicompact. Exercises: Show composition of two quasicompact morphisms is quasicompact (7.3.A); show any morphism from a Noetherian scheme is quasicompact (7.3.B(a)); quasicompactness is affine-local on the target (7.3.C(a)). Warning/caution: quasicompact source and target do not force the morphism to be quasicompact (counterexample in 7.3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiseparated morphism / scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Y is quasiseparated if for every affine open subset U of Y, π^{-1}(U) is a quasiseparated scheme (definition used as a hypothesis for morphisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use together with quasicompactness (qcqs). Many common morphisms (locally Noetherian source, affine, separated) are quasiseparated. Exercises: composition of quasiseparated morphisms is true but nontrivial (mentioned in 7.3.B and 7.3.2); quasiseparatedness is affine-local on the target (7.3.C(b)). Practical note: readers working only with locally Noetherian schemes may assume quasiseparatedness as a standing hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qcqs (quasicompact and quasiseparated) lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a quasicompact quasiseparated scheme and s ∈ Γ(X, O_X), then the natural map Γ(X, O_X)_s → Γ(X_s, O_X) is an isomorphism (7.3.5). X_s denotes the locus where s doesn't vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation/proof sketch: cover X by finitely many affine opens Ui = Spec Ai, then use exactness of Čech-type sequence and localization commuting with finite products; quasiseparatedness supplies finite covers of intersections. Exercises: 7.3.E asks to identify the natural map. The lemma is used repeatedly to justify qcqs hypotheses in later arguments (and to get finite products commuting with localization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is affine if for every affine open set U of Y, π^{-1}(U) (interpreted as an open subscheme of X) is an affine scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trivial facts: compositions of affine morphisms are affine. Affine morphisms are quasicompact and quasiseparated (7.3.D). Affine-locality on the target: a morphism is affine if there is a cover of Y by affine opens U such that π^{-1}(U) is affine (Proposition 7.3.4). Proofs rely on the Affine Communication Lemma 5.3.2 and the Qcqs Lemma. Exercises and consequences: useful exercises (7.3.F) show complements of locally principal closed subsets in affine schemes are affine; affineness having non-obvious consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-locality of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties such as quasicompactness, quasiseparatedness, afﬁneness, locally finite type/presentation are affine-local on the target: they can be checked on an affine open cover of the target (see Exercises 7.3.C, Proposition 7.3.4, 7.3.O, 7.3.T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guiding principle: reduce checking of many morphism properties to affine pieces and use algebra. Frequently used in proofs (apply Affine Communication Lemma). Exercises explicitly ask to show the affine-local nature for specific properties (7.3.C, 7.3.G, 7.3.O, 7.3.T).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is finite if for every affine open set Spec B of Y, π^{-1}(Spec B) is the spectrum of a B-algebra that is a finitely generated B-module. By definition, finite morphisms are affine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology warning: 'finite' (A finite B-algebra = finitely generated as a B-module) vs 'finitely generated' as an algebra (weaker). Examples: branched covers (k[t] over k[u] via polynomial p(t)), closed embeddings Spec A/I → Spec A, normalization examples. Properties: finite morphisms are quasicompact, quasiseparated, closed maps (images of closed sets are closed, Exercise 7.3.M), finite-to-one (Exercise 7.3.K), and have finite fibers. Composition of finite morphisms is finite (7.3.I). Exercises: finite morphisms to Spec k give discrete finite unions of points with finite residue fields (7.3.H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite = integral + finite type
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism is finite if and only if it is integral and of finite type (7.3.P(b)). Also finite morphisms are of finite type (7.3.P(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights the algebraic decomposition: integrality (every induced ring map is integral) plus finite type together imply finiteness. Use Exercises 7.2 and 7.3 to manipulate these notions; the converse direction and proofs are exercises in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is integral if it is affine and for every affine open subset Spec B ⊂ Y with π^{-1}(Spec B) = Spec A, the induced map B → A is integral (i.e., elements of A satisfy monic relations over B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affine-local condition (Exercises 7.2.A, 7.2.B, Affine Communication Lemma). Integral morphisms are closed (exercise 7.3.M; use Lying Over Theorem 7.2.5). Note: finite ⇒ integral, but integral need not be finite (example Spec Q → Spec Q). Fibers of integral morphisms have special topological property: no point is in the closure of another (7.3.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally of finite type / finite type morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: π : X → Y is locally of finite type if for every affine open Spec B of Y and every affine open Spec A in π^{-1}(Spec B), the induced map B → A expresses A as a finitely generated B-algebra. π is of finite type if it is locally of finite type and quasicompact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: π^{-1}(Spec B) can be covered by affine opens Spec Ai with each Ai a finitely generated B-algebra. Examples: the structure morphism P^n_A → Spec A is of finite type. Composition and local properties: open embeddings are locally of finite type; compositions preserve locally finite type (7.3.Q). Exercise 7.3.P discusses relation with finiteness/integrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally of finite presentation / finite presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring A is finitely presented over B if A ≅ B[x1,...,xn]/(r1,...,rj) (finite generators and finite relations). A morphism π : X → Y is locally of finite presentation if for each affine open Spec B of Y, π^{-1}(Spec B) = ∪ Spec Ai with each Ai finitely presented over B. Finite presentation = locally finite presentation + quasicompact + quasiseparated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Y is locally Noetherian, locally of finite presentation = locally of finite type and finite presentation = finite type. This notion is well-motivated for non-Noetherian situations (exercise 9.3.H and 7.3.U). Properties: affine-local on target and on source (7.3.T, 7.3.U); open embeddings and compositions preserve (7.3.V, 7.3.W). Remark: characterization as limit-preserving (Hom commutes with limits) (7.3.18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiﬁnite morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π is quasiﬁnite if it is of finite type and for all q ∈ Y, the fiber π^{-1}(q) is a finite set (7.3.14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main point: finite fibers; finite type ensures good behavior under base change. Finite implies quasiﬁnite (combining 7.3.K and 7.3.P(a)), but there are quasiﬁnite morphisms that are not finite (example A^2_k - {(0,0)} → A^2_k has finite fibers but is not finite). Quasiﬁnite morphisms to Spec k are finite (7.4.D). Visualization: think of quasiﬁnite as a finite map with some (closed locus of) points removed; Zariski's Main Theorem connects this to finite maps (7.3.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibers and finite fibers
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite morphisms have finite fibers (Exercise 7.3.K). Integral morphisms need not have finite fibers, but their fibers have the property that no point is in the closure of another point (7.3.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints for proving finite fibers: reduce to affine case X = Spec A, Y = Spec B, mod out by prime q ⊂ B to reduce to fiber Spec(A/π♯ q A) and then to generic point by localization. See Exercise 7.3.K for details. Examples illustrating difference between finite fibers and finiteness: open embeddings with finite fibers but not finite (7.3.9, 7.3.L).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructible subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructible subset of a Noetherian topological space is a member of the smallest family containing all opens and closed under finite intersection and complement. Equivalently, finite disjoint unions of locally closed subsets (7.4.A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: preimage of a constructible set under a continuous map of Noetherian spaces is constructible. Exercises: show constructible subset is closed iff stable under specialization and open iff stable under generization (7.4.C). Use in Chevalley: images of morphisms are constructible in finite type Noetherian setting (7.4.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevalley’s Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is a finite type morphism of Noetherian schemes, the image of any constructible set is constructible. In particular, the image of π is constructible (7.4.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: immediate proof of Nullstellensatz (7.4.3). Proof strategy in text: reduce to affine irreducible Y, apply Generic Freeness Lemma to get dense open subset on which image either contains it or is disjoint (7.4.L), use Noetherian induction (7.4.N, 7.4.O). Exercises guide completing the proof (7.4.M–7.4.O).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grothendieck’s Generic Freeness Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose B is a Noetherian integral domain. Then every finitely generated B-algebra satisfies (†): for each finitely generated A-module M there exists a nonzero f ∈ B such that M_f is a free B_f-module (7.4.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof is given as a sequence of exercises (7.4.F–7.4.K). Uses induction on number of generators, analyze ascending chain of submodules in M viewed as A[T]-module, use localization and finite isomorphism classes (7.4.G–7.4.J). Application: in proof of Chevalley (7.4.L) to find dense open where image behavior is uniform (either contains D(f) or disjoint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of quantifiers / Fundamental Theorem of Elimination Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Given polynomials f1,...,fp, g1,...,gq ∈ k[W1,...,Wm,X1,...,Xn] over an algebraically closed field k, there exists a Zariski-constructible subset Y ⊂ k^m such that (w1,...,wm) ∈ Y iff there exists (x1,...,xn) solving f_i(...)=0 and g_j(...)�=0 (7.4.5 / 7.4.P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint/approach: view the solution set as a locally closed subset X of A^{m+n}, consider the projection π_cl on closed points, and apply Chevalley to see projection of constructible set is constructible. This is the algebraic statement that solvability conditions on coefficients are algebraic (no exotic functions needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frobenius morphism properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For k of characteristic p and φ: k[x1,...,xn] → k[x1,...,xn] given by φ(xi)=xi^p, the induced morphism F: A^n_k → A^n_k satisfies: Fr is identity on underlying sets only for suitable power; F can be bijective but not an isomorphism of schemes (7.3.16, 7.3.R, 7.3.S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: show Fr is identity on sets but not morphism; show F is bijection but not isomorphism; absolute Frobenius for schemes over F_p defined by f ↦ f^p on rings (7.3.S). These illustrate subtleties between underlying topological behavior and scheme-theoretic structure.
